sec.title: Background
sec.p: Metabolic pathways are known to significantly impact the development and advancement of lung cancer. This study sought to establish a signature related to butyrate metabolism that is specifically linked to lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: For the purpose of identifying butyrate metabolism-related differentially expressed genes (BMR-DEGs) in the TCGA-LUAD dataset, we introduced transcriptome data. This was followed by the implementation of the univariate Cox and LASSO analyses in order to construct a LUAD gene signature. We performed a comprehensive analysis of gene function enrichment between the two populations at risk, thoroughly examined their immune microenvironment characteristics, and assessed the effectiveness of immunotherapy. Finally, the function of CDKN3 in LUAD was verified by in vitro experiments.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Through a comprehensive analysis of the TCGA-LUAD dataset, 51 significant BMR-DEGs were confirmed. Subsequently, five characteristic genes, CPS1, ABCC2, CDKN3, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1 were identified to create prognostic features for butyrate metabolism related outcomes in LUAD. Cox regression analysis determined that the pathological T stage, tumor stage, and RiskScore could serve as independent prognostic indicators. Analysis of the abundance of 22 immune infiltrating cells revealed that 15 immune cell types exhibited substantial differences and were strongly associated with risk ratings and prognosis. An important correlation exists between risk ratings and immunological checkpoints, which can be utilized to forecast the efficacy of treatment. In the high-risk group, there was an upregulation of the expression of PD-L2, PD-L1, and PD-1. Additionally, the risk score showed a positive correlation with TIDE and Exclusion score, while showing a negative correlation with Dysfunction score. Furthermore, the IC50 values for cisplatin, paclitaxel, and docetaxel were notably elevated in the high-risk group, indicating that these medications could potentially provide therapeutic advantages for this particular group. Finally, we determined that knockdown CDKN3 inhibited the proliferation and metastasis of LUAD cells.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We identify and validate a novel BMR-related prognostic signature comprising 5 DEGs for LUAD patients. Our data might provide a new molecular target for LUAD treatment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Lung cancer has a high morbidity and mortality rate in the world and is the most common malignant tumor. Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), which accounts for nearly 40% of all lung cancer cases worldwide, has become a health challenge that cannot be ignored. According to estimates from the American Cancer Society, by the end of 2023, approximately 127,070 deaths may occur due to lung cancer, constituting 20% of the total cancer mortality rate, with LUAD being the prevailing subtype of lung cancer [1–3]. LUAD is characterized by difficulties in early detection, rapid tumor progression, and low rates of surgical resection in advanced stages, leading to a poorer prognosis for patients in the intermediate and late stages [4]. However, with advancements in diagnostic and therapeutic technologies, clinical management of lung cancer has gradually shifted towards precision and personalized treatments [5]. Among these, immunotherapy has been recognized as an effective treatment modality for various advanced and aggressive cancers [6–8], with the “immunotherapy +” approach targeting PD-1/PD-L1 becoming a prominent direction in cancer therapy [9]. Research on immunotherapy as monotherapy or in combination with chemotherapy has shown promising results in improving prognosis and overcoming drug resistance, although the overall benefit for the majority of lung cancer patients remains limited [10]. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms underlying the occurrence of LUAD and the tumor microenvironment in relation to immunotherapy is crucial for identifying more effective treatment strategies.

Alterations in the gut microbiota and its metabolites can cause changes in intestinal inflammation and immunological responses, which can in turn promote the development of cancer [11]. Butyrate is a significant byproduct of the gut microbiota. It has a role in regulating the gut microbiota, maintaining intestinal balance, and is also implicated in tumor development through many mechanisms [12, 13]. Butyrate is essential for the metabolic processes of cells in the colon. As the primary source of energy, it not only supplies the required energy for cells in the colon, but also plays an active role in preserving the integrity of the intestinal mucosal lining through several processes such as immune response, gene expression, and epigenetic control. This maintenance impact contributes to the mitigation of intestinal inflammation, thereby diminishing the likelihood of developing cancer [14]. Butyrate has the ability to greatly enhance the effectiveness of anti-PD-1 therapy by improving the functionality of CD8 + T cells [15]. Studies on rectal cancer have demonstrated that butyrate, when examined through metabolomics and proteomics research, can modify cellular metabolism, suppress the Warburg effect, and facilitate the dephosphorylation and tetramerization of PKM2. As a result, it hinders the growth of rectal cancer tumor cells [16]. Scientists have conducted research on the impact of butyrate and its analog, 3-bromopyruvate (3-BP), on breast cancer cells. The findings indicate that butyrate can augment the cytotoxicity of 3-BP by accelerating the rate at which MCT1/4 is transported, suppressing the Warburg effect, and triggering apoptosis [17]. Butyrate is a byproduct of the microbial community in the colon that is produced by fermentation. In mice, it has been observed that it can induce the differentiation of colonic Treg cells, which may be beneficial for treating colitis and potentially maintaining immune system homeostasis by altering the acetylation of histone H3 during Treg cell differentiation [18]. Recent research has revealed a strong correlation between genes involved in butyrate metabolism and the development of cancers including cervical cancer and liver cancer [19, 20]. Nevertheless, there is a scarcity of research that thoroughly examines the biomarker potential of butyrate metabolism-related genes (BMRGs) in predicting prognosis in LUAD.

This work employed a range of bioinformatics techniques, utilizing data from various sources, to examine the specific features of changes in butyrate metabolism in LUAD. Afterwards, we developed and confirmed gene characteristics related to butyrate metabolism to predict the prognosis of LUAD. We analyzed the variations in butyrate metabolism and immunological composition between low-risk and high-risk groups. Additionally, we have successfully developed a prognostic model called the “butyrate score” that accurately predicts the prognosis of LUAD. In addition, we investigated the usefulness of our butyrate score in predicting the responses of LUAD patients to immunotherapy and medication sensitivity. Additional in vitro cell tests were performed to examine the function of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 3 (CDKN3), a pivotal gene, in the model. Our findings might provide a potentially valuable biomarker for LUAD patients with a strong predictive value that can help develop personalized therapeutic approaches.

sec.title: Public data collection
sec.p: LUAD RNA sequencing data were obtained from the cancer genome atlas (TCGA) database (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/) was used as training set, which included survival information from 59 adjacent normal tissue and 526 tumor samples. The GSE68465 dataset containing information on 443 cases from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) was used as the validation set. 347 BMRGs (correlation score>7) were identified using the GeneCards database (http://www.genecards.org/).

sec.title: Differential expression analysis of BMRGs
sec.p: The differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the TCGA-LUAD dataset was analyzed utilizing the ‘DESeq2’ program (version 1.36.0) [21], with threshold values were set at adj.p.value < 0.05 and |log2FC| > 2. The DEGs connected to butyrate metabolism, known as BMR-DEGs, were identified by overlapping the DEGs and the genes involved in BMRGs. The BMR-DEGs were visualized using the Volcano plot and heatmap. The volcano plot was drawn using the ‘ggplot2’ package (version 3.4.0) [22] to visualize the BMR-DEGs. The ‘pheatmap’ package (version 1.0.12) was used to build heatmaps, which visually represent the variations in gene expression levels. We utilized the ‘clusterProfiler’ tool (version 4.4.4) [23] to conduct Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis of BMR-DEGs. p.adjust < 0.05 was selected as criterion.

sec.title: Risk score-based subgroup analysis of LUAD patients
sec.p: TCGA-LUAD dataset was used as the training set and univariate Cox regression analysis and LASSO regression analysis was performed to identify BMR-DEGs that are strongly associated with prognosis. The risk score model calculating formula was:

According to the median risk score, the LUAD patients were classify into high-risk group and low-risk group. To validate the capability of the prognostic risk score model, the Kaplan-Meier survival curve was performed by R software “survival” package to assess the difference in survival between high- and low-risk groups. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of 1-, 2- and 3‐year survival was performed by “survival ROC” package in R, and the areas under curve (AUC) was calculated to evaluate the sensitivity of the model. The relationship between risk score and prognostic genes was evaluated using the Spearman correlation approach. Furthermore, the GSE68465 dataset was employed as an external validation set for the risk model in order to further confirm the reliability and predictive capability of the model. In order to investigate the connection between prognostic genes and clinical characteristics, we conducted a thorough analysis of the gene expression in several clinicopathological variables, such as age, sex, and important factors like N, T, and M in the pathological stage.

sec.title: Clinical nomogram model
sec.p: The study conducted univariate and multivariate Cox analysis to discover independent prognostic indicators. The analysis covered many parameters such as tumor stage, pathological N stage, T stage, M stage, and risk score. Afterwards, we constructed a nomogram using these independent parameters that influence the survival of patients with lung cancer. This nomogram provides a visual prediction of the chance of survival at 1, 2, and 3 years. Furthermore, we conducted an unbiased assessment of the nomogram’s predictive capability using calibration curves to verify the precision and dependability of its predictions.

sec.title: Gene set enrichment analysis
sec.p: We utilized the ‘DESeq2’ software program (version 1.36.0) [21] to conduct differential analysis of gene expression data between the two risk groupings. The objective was to identify genes that were expressed differently in these subgroups. Afterwards, using KEGG gene sets, we conducted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) to uncover gene expression patterns associated with certain biological pathways or activities in different risk categories [23]. During the enrichment analysis, a significance criterion of adjusted p-value less than 0.05 was employed to identify enrichment pathways that were statistically significant.

sec.title: Estimation of immune features and analysis of chemotherapy
sec.p: We employed the CIBERSORT algorithm [24] to precisely determine the expression levels of 22 immune cells in the microenvironment of lung cancer. Afterwards, we performed a thorough examination of the connection between these distinct immune cells and the risk score. We calculated the correlation coefficient between them to uncover the possible association between immune cell infiltration and the chance of developing lung adenocarcinoma. Meanwhile, the study employed K-M analysis to investigate the correlation between specific differential immune cells and the prognosis of individuals diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. In order to investigate possible connections between immunological checkpoints and TIDE with risk ratings, we conducted a Spearman’s rank-correlation study. This approach has the capability to uncover the magnitude and orientation of the connection between variables. Furthermore, we conducted a thorough examination of immune checkpoint expression in the two categories with different levels of risk. Furthermore, the inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 4 drugs (Cisplatin, Paclitaxel, Docetaxel and Gefitinib) of two risk subgroups was calculated by ‘pRRophetic’ package in GDSC database.

sec.title: Construction of ceRNA network
sec.p: In order to build the competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network, we primarily employed microRNA (miRNA) and long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) data extracted from the TCGA-LUAD dataset. We utilized the ‘DESeq2’ software program (version 1.36.0) [21] to conduct a comprehensive analysis of miRNA and lncRNA expression levels in order to uncover the disparities in expression of these non-coding RNAs in distinct risk subgroups of lung adenocarcinoma. The correlation between differential miRNAs and prognostic genes was calculated, and negatively correlated miRNA-mRNA pairs were selected for subsequent analysis. Using the StarBase database, we employed clip-Exp ≥ 1 and pan-cancer ≥ 0 as screening criteria to identify miRNAs that are linked to prognostic genes. Subsequently, we compared these miRNAs with those linked to prognostic genes in order to identify the shared miRNAs. Additionally, we employed the identical approach to screen and acquire the overlapping long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). Using the intersecting non-coding RNA and mRNA data, we created lncRNA-mRNA-miRNA networks to uncover their interaction linkages. Ultimately, we employed Cytoscape software to enhance and depict the network outcomes, so enhancing the clarity and comprehensibility of the network structure.

sec.title: Cell culture and cell transfection
sec.p: The BEAS-2B, A549, H1650, H1975, and H1299 cells were cultivated in DMEM medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, USA) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin in a humidified 37 °C incubator with a 5% CO2 atmosphere.

For silencing CDKN3, two small interfering RNA (siRNA) sequences against CDKN3 (siCDKN3#1 and siCDKN3#2) and negative control (siNC) sequence were designed and synthesized by GenePharma (Shanghai, China). A549 and H1299 cells were transfected with indicated siRNA using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocols.

sec.title: Real-time PCR and RNA extraction
sec.p: RNAs were extracted from cells using TRIzol reagent (Tiangen Biochem Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). RNA was converted into cDNA applying the Takara Prime Script RT Kit (TaKaRa Bio Inc., China). Quantitative PCR was applied using SYBR® Premix Ex Taq™ II kit (TaKaRa) on a Real-Time system (Bio-Rad, CA, USA). Relative RNA level of CDKN3 were calculated following the 2−ΔΔCt method, where GAPDH served as the internal control. The CDKN3 primer sequences used were as follows: sense strand, 5′-GCACTGGTCTCGACGTGGG-3′; antisense strand, 5′-ACCTGGAAGAGCACATAAACCGA-3′.

sec.title: Western blotting
sec.p: LUAD tissues or cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (Beyotime) and protein concentration was determined using a BCA kit (Thermo Fisher). Protein extracts were loaded and separated on SDS-PAGE gels and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore, MA, USA). Nonspecific interactions were blocked with 5% skim milk for 1 h. After washing with TBST buffer, the membranes were incubated with primary antibodies CDKN3 (cat#: ab175393, 1/5000, Abcam, MA, USA) and GAPDH (cat#: AB0036, 1/10000, Abways, Shanghai, China) overnight at 4℃. After washing, the membranes were further incubated with HRP-labeled secondary antibody (cat#: ab205718, 1/10000, Abcam) 1 h at room temperature. The signal was visualized by ECL reagent (Thermo Fisher) and the gray value was digitized by ImageJ software.

sec.title: Immunohistochemical (IHC) assay
sec.p: From January 2020 to December 2021, Hebei Chest Hospital surgically treated and pathologically confirmed 36 cases of LUAD tissue specimens for this study. Additionally, normal tissues adjacent to the tumor at a distance of more than 5 cm were selected as the adjacent normal group (36 cases). The Review Committee of Hebei Chest Hospital has approved this study. We embedded the tumors and their corresponding surrounding tissues from the 36 individuals mentioned above in paraffin and divided them into sections. Subsequently, the membrane was incubated with a dilution ratio of 1:200 of the CDKN3 antibody (cat#: DF6791, Affinity Biosciences) and a dilution ratio of 1:500 of the appropriate secondary antibody (cat#: BE0101, Bioeasy). Two pathologists independently evaluated the staining results.

sec.title: CCK8 and colony formation assays
sec.p: The cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8, Wuhan Pronomai Biotech Co., LTD., China) was employed to identify cell proliferation. Cells were placed in 96-well plates and exposed to CCK-8 reagent for a duration of 2 h. The absorbance at 450 nm (OD450) was measured.

The clonogenic capacity of LUAD cells was evaluated using a colony formation test. Monolayers consisting of 2 × 103 cells per well were added to six-well plates. Following a two-week incubation period, cells were treated with methanol for 15 min. Subsequently, cells were supplied with 0.5% crystal violet solution (Beijing, China) for 15 min. Ultimately, the dyed colonies were enumerated using a light microscope to acquire a precise count of colonies.

sec.title: Cell migration and invasion assays
sec.p: We assessed cell migration and invasion using a previously reported protocol [25]. Matrigel-coated Transwell chambers (Corning, NY, USA) was utilized to measure cell invasion. 500 µL of complete DMEM medium was put into the lower chamber. And the upper chamber was introduced with LUAD cells (2.5 × 104 cells). Following a 24 h-incubation, cells attached to the lower surface were fixed with methanol for 10 min and stained for 20 min with 0.1% crystal violet. Finally, the cells that exhibited positive staining were observed using a microscope. The cell migration assay was performed in the same manner as the cell invasion assay except that the chambers without Matrigel coated.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed with R (version 3.6.1) and SPSS (version 23.0). The expression of CDKN3 in unpaired samples was analyzed using the Wilcoxon rank sum test, whereas the Wilcoxon signed rank sum test was utilized to evaluate the expression in paired samples. The Kruskal-Wallis test, Wilcoxon signed rank sum test, and χ2 test were employed to examine the association between clinicopathological characteristics and CDKN3 expression. Data of cell experiment were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. For the comparisons between groups, student’s t-test and one-way ANOVA were performed. p < 0.05 (two-sided) was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Identification of BMR-DEGs in LUAD
sec.p: Through a comprehensive examination of the TCGA-LUAD database, we have identified 51 genes that are differentially expressed and have a tight association with basal metabolic rate (BMR, referred to as BMR-DEGs). Among these genes, 33 were found to be significantly up-regulated, while 18 were significantly down-regulated (Fig. 1A and C). In order to gain a deeper understanding of the biological activities of these BMR-DEGs, we conducted functional enrichment analysis. The GO results indicated that they mostly had a role in the regulation of bone remodeling, as shown in Fig. 1D. The KEGG analysis revealed that the differentially expressed genes associated with the BMR were primarily concentrated in the crucial pathways of “steroid hormone production” and “cytochrome P450 metabolism of xenobiotics” (Fig. 1E). This suggests that these genes have a significant role in regulating hormone balance and the metabolism of xenobiotics.

caption.p: Differentially expressed butyrate metabolism-related genes (BMR-DEGs) in LUAD. (A) The interaction between BMRGs and DEGs. (B) BMR-DEGs volcano plot. The vertical axis represents the corrected p value, the horizontal axis represents log2FC, red represents upregulated genes, and blue represents downregulated genes. (C) The heatmap of the 51 BMR-DEGs. Each column represents one sample, with green in the first row indicating healthy samples and orange indicating diseased samples; Each behavior represents one gene, with red indicating upregulation and blue indicating downregulation; The middle color represents the relative expression level of a gene in a sample. (D-E) Enrichment analysis using the GO database and KEGG database. The vertical axis represents the pathway name, and the horizontal axis represents the proportion of enriched genes. The larger the bubble, the more enriched genes there are. The color changes from blue to red, indicating increasing significance

sec.title: Prognostic signature based on BMR-DEGs associated with survival
sec.p: In the TCGA-LUAD dataset, six genes were found to be significant (HR ≠ 1 and P < 0.05) through univariate regression analysis. These genes are F2, CPS1, ABCC2, CDKN3, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1 (Fig. 2A). Using LASSO regression analysis, we conducted a thorough examination of six significant genes in order to uncover the optimal ones. Finally, five feature genes were identified, namely CPS1, ABCC2, CDKN3, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1 (Fig. 2B and C). In addition, these five genes were chosen as prognostic genes to create a prognostic signature for BM-related outcomes in LUAD. After analyzing Fig. 2D and E, LUAD patients were carefully classified into two risk groups for more accurate analysis and research. The high-risk group showed a concentrated expression of five prognostic genes (Fig. 2F and G). Remarkably, there were notable survival differences observed between two distinct risk groups. Significantly reduced survival rates were seen in individuals belonging to the high-risk LUAD group, as demonstrated in Fig. 2H and I. In order to evaluate the dependability of the model, we analyzed the AUC values in the TCGA database to predict the survival rates at 1, 2, and 3 years in patients with LUAD. The results indicated that the AUC values for predicting the survival of LUAD patients were 0.68, 0.68, and 0.676, respectively. These findings, as depicted in Fig. 2J, demonstrate that our model possesses a certain level of accuracy and dependability. An external validation dataset (GSE68465) was used to further validate the risk model. Consistent with the results observed in TCGA dataset, LUAD patients in the high-risk group had significantly worse overall survival. Specifically, AUC values exceeded 0.60 at 1, 2, and 3 years, as shown in Fig. 2K, which further confirms the validity and robustness of our risk model in predicting survival in patients with LUAD.

caption.p: BMR-DEG prognostic labels and six risk signatures. (A) Forest plot of BMR-DEG gene prognostic value. When HR > 1, it indicates that the exposure factor is a promoting factor for the occurrence of positive (death) events. (B-C) Lasso regression analysis was performed to select feature genes and build a Lasso model employing 5 BMR-DEGs. (D-E) Patient risk score and survival status scatter plot. (F-G) Heatmap of five BMR-DEGs expression. (H-I) KM survival curves of TCGA training set and GEO validation set. (J-K) Training and testing cohort time-dependent ROC curves

sec.title: Prognostic analysis of patients with lung adenocarcinoma
sec.p: The Cox regression analysis identified tumor stage, RiskScore, and pathological T stage as the primary factors that independently influence the prognosis of LUAD patients (p < 0.05, Fig. 3A and B). A nomogram was created to display the survival rates at 1, 2, and 3 years (Fig. 3C). The calibration curve demonstrated the efficacy of the nomogram (Fig. 3D).

caption.p: Validation of prognostic models. (A-B) Multivariate and univariate Cox regression analysis. (C-D) Nomogram incorporating multiple clinicopathological features, with calibration and C-index assessment to evaluate the consistency between predicted and actual survival rates

sec.title: Immune microenvironment of LUAD
sec.p: To further explore the immune environment of LUAD, we analyzed the expression of 22 immune cells in two sample groups in TCGA dataset (Fig. 4A). The study identified 15 immune cell types that exhibited significant differences in abundance. These included naive B cells, gamma delta T cells, CD8 T cells, CD4 memory resting T cells, CD4 memory activated T cells, resting NK cells, monocytes, activated NK cells, M0 Macrophages, M1 Macrophages, resting dendritic cells, activated dendritic cells, resting mast cells, neutrophils, and activated mast cells (Fig. 4B). The expression levels of M0 macrophages and CD4 memory activated T cells were positively correlated with the risk score. The study found a negative correlation between riskscore and the levels of resting dendritic cells, resting mast cells, andCD4 memory resting T cells (Fig. 4C). The K-M survival analysis revealed that four distinct immune cell types (M0 Macrophages, CD4 memory activated T cells, resting dendritic cells, and CD4 memory resting T cells) were shown to be correlated with prognosis (Fig. 4D), with only “Mast cell resting” P = 0.062 greater than 0.05, which was not significantly correlated with prognosis.

caption.p: Illustrates the correlation between BMR-DEGs and the infiltration of immune cells. (A-B) Infiltration levels of 22 immune cells in groups with different risk levels. A: The horizontal axis represents the sample, and the vertical axis represents the proportion of immune infiltrating cells. Different colors indicate different immune infiltrating cells; B: *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ns: no significant. (C) The risk model is connected to the immune cells in LUAD. |R |>0.3 and p < 0.05 were considered to be correlated. (D) The presence of tumor immune cells is linked to prognosis. p < 0.05, was considered that the immune cell is related to prognosis

sec.title: The relationship between risk scores and immune checkpoints
sec.p: Additionally, we observed substantial positive associations between the risk score and the four immunological checkpoints (Fig. 5A). PD-L2, PD-L1, and PD-1 exhibited increased expression in the high-risk group (p < 0.05, Fig. 5B). Our analysis revealed significant differences in the scores of TIDE, Exclusion, and Dysfunction between the two groups. Furthermore, we observed a positive association between the risk score and the TIDE and Exclusion scores. The risk score had a negative correlation with the dysfunction score, as shown in Fig. 5C. To identify possible medications that target prognostic genes, we conducted a comparison of the IC50 values of four pharmaceuticals across two risk categories. As shown in Fig. 5D, the IC50 values for cisplatin, paclitaxel, and docetaxel were all significantly higher in the high-risk group compared with the low-risk group (p < 0.001 and p < 0.01).

caption.p: Shows the correlation between BMR-DEGs and the sensitivity of immunotherapy and chemotherapy. (A–B) Distribution of four commonly observed immune checkpoint genes in populations with varying levels of risk. (C) Examining the association between risk scores and TIDE, Exclusion, and Dysfunction scores. R > 0 indicates positive correlation, R < 0 indicates negative correlation, |R|<0.3 indicates weak correlation. (D) IC50 values of three commonly used chemotherapy drugs in high and low risk populations were compared

sec.title: The ceRNA network analysis
sec.p: The ceRNA network was used to explore the regulatory mechanism of CPS1, ABCC2, CDKN3, SLC2A1 and IGFBP1. We successfully identified 340 differentially expressed mirnas in two different risk subgroups. We selected 278 miRNAs that had a negative correlation with those genes. Using the intersection operation, we matched the predicted miRNAs in the StarBase database with the negatively correlated miRNAs and identified 27 common miRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 6A). In addition, we identified 17 long non-coding RNAs (Supplementary Fig. 6B). Afterwards, we created the ceRNA network (Fig. 6A), consisting of 49 nodes and 77 edges. In this network, we found that CDKN3 was linked to hsa-mir-146b, hsa-mir-5581 influenced the expression of IGFBP1, and hsa-mir-32 controlled the expression of cps1. Ultimately, we conducted a thorough examination of the correlation between prognostic genes and clinical characteristics. Among the five prognostic genes, CPS1, ABCC2, CDKN3, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1 exhibited higher expression in the LUAD group (Fig. 6B). Additionally, the overexpression of CDKN3, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1 genes was associated with more severe clinical staging and poorer clinical outcomes in patients (Fig. 6C and D).

caption.p: Construction of a ceRNA network of prognostic genes and clinical prognosis. (A) Construction of a ceRNA network of prognostic genes. Purple represents hub genes; Green represents miRNA; Orange represents lncRNA. (B) Differences in gene expression levels between tumor samples and normal samples. (C) Correlation between gene expression levels and clinical stage. (D) Survival curves of CDKN3, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1 in high and low-risk groups

sec.title: CDKN3 was upregulated in LUAD
sec.p: To further validate the expression of CDKN3 in LUAD tissues, we used 36 samples of LUAD and matched normal adjacent tissues to detect the expression of CDKN3 protein through IHC. Based on the staining intensity, we classified the expression of CDKN3 into negative, weakly positive, moderately positive, and strongly positive categories. The results indicated that the CDKN3 protein was primarily located in the cytoplasm of cells (Fig. 7A). Among the 36 samples of normal adjacent tissues, 22 cases (61.1%) were negative, 12 cases (33.3%) were weakly positive, and 2 cases (5.6%) were moderately positive. CDKN3 expression was detected to varying degrees in 36 cancer tissue samples. More precisely, out of the total of 36 cases, 10 cases (27.8%) had negative results, 17 cases (47.2%) had weak positive results, 6 cases (16.7%) had moderate positive results, and 3 cases (8.3%) had strong positive results. Through the utilization of a rank-sum test analysis, we have determined that the expression level of CDKN3 in lung cancer tissues is notably elevated compared to that in neighboring normal tissues (p < 0.001, Fig. 7B). The Western blot study results confirmed that the expression level of CDKN3 in lung cancer tissues matched the findings from the prior IHC analysis, suggesting that CDKN3 was upregulated in LUAD tissues (p < 0.001, Fig. 7C). Additionally, Western blot and qPCR confirmed that the protein and mRNA levels of CDKN3 were higher in multiple human LUAD cell lines compared to normal lung cells (p < 0.05, p < 0.01 and p < 0.001, Fig. 7D and E). Therefore, CDKN3 may promote the development of LUAD and serve as a potential prognostic biomarker.

caption.p: CDKN3 expression in LUAD tissues. (A) The expression of CDKN3 in LUAD and adjacent tissues was detected by IHC. (B) IHC score. (C) The protein expression of CDKN3 in LUAD and adjacent tissues was detected by Western blot. (D-E) The protein and mRNA expression of CDKN3 in lung cancer cells was identified using Western blot and qPCR methods. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01 and ***p < 0.001 vs. Normal or BEAS-2B group

sec.title: CDKN3 promoted the proliferation of LUAD cells
sec.p: This study aims to further examine the impact of CDKN3 on the proliferation of lung cancer cells. We noticed a notable increase in the levels of CDKN3 protein expression in A549 and H1299 cells. Therefore, siCDKN3 was used to infect A549 and H1299 cells, and the knockdown efficiency of CDKN3 in these cells after lentivirus infection was detected by western blot and qPCR (p < 0.001, Fig. 8A). We performed the CCK-8 assay to verify whether the downregulation of CDKN3 affects the proliferative capacity of LUAD cells. As shown in Fig. 8B, CDKN3 accelerated the growth of LUAD cells (p < 0.001). Furthermore, in the clone formation experiment, knockdown of CDKN3 significantly reduced the clone formation ability of A549 and H1299 cells (p < 0.001, Fig. 8C). These results indicate that CDKN3 promotes the proliferation of LUAD cells.

caption.p: CDKN3 silencing suppressed LUAD cell proliferation. (A) Downregulation of CDKN3 and its transfection efficiency in A549 and H1299 cells. (B) Cell viability of A549 and H1299 cells detected by the CCK-8 assay. (C) Clone formation assay to assess the proliferation of LUAD cells. ***p < 0.001 vs. siNC group

sec.title: CDKN3 promoted migration and invasion of LUAD cells
sec.p: In order to further examine the correlation between CDKN3 and LUAD cell migration, we conducted a wound healing test. The results showed that the wound healing speed was faster in CDKN3-silenced A549 and H1299 cells (p < 0.001, Fig. 9A and D), suggesting that CDKN3 is associated with the migration ability of A549 and H1299 cells. We conducted a transwell experiment to further confirm the impact of CDKN3 on the migratory and invasive characteristics of lung cancer cells. Consistent with the findings of the wound healing assay, the CDKN3 knockdown group exhibited a reduced number of cells moving through the bottom chamber compared to the control group in both A549 and H1299 cells (p < 0.001, Fig. 9E and H). These results indicate that CDKN3 is an oncogene in LUAD.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Butyrate is a constituent of the gastrointestinal microbial community. The intestinal microbiome is essential for maintaining human health as it aids in the digestion of food, production of vitamins, and regulation of the immune system [11]. Studies have indicated that butyrate has a notable anti-tumor effect in several types of cancers, including colon cancer and stomach cancer [26, 27]. Therefore, it can be speculated that butyrate has potential value as an anti-tumor drug. Several studies have demonstrated that butyrate can impede the advancement of cancers by various methods. Butyrate has multiple anti-tumor effects. It can inhibit the growth of tumor cells, induce programmed cell death, and even regulate and enhance the body’s immune response against tumors [28]. Research has indicated that butyrate can impact the efficacy of immunotherapy in solid tumors. Additionally, butyrate is believed to be a chemical that modulates the immune response and has the potential to augment the efficiency of immunotherapy [29]. Nevertheless, a thorough investigation into the significance of butyrate metabolic pathways in relation to the prognosis and systemic treatment of lung adenocarcinoma is lacking. To fully understand the function of the butyrate metabolism pathway in lung cancer, we must investigate its role and mechanism in early detection, prognostic evaluation, and systemic treatment. This understanding will facilitate its more effective implementation in future clinical practice.

Initially, the TCGA database was utilized to identify 296 genes that were differentially expressed (referred to as BMRGs) between tumor and normal tissues (Fig. 1). This screening process served as the foundation for further study. Next, Cox regression analysis was employed to discover the genes that are linked to butyrate. Subsequently, LASSO regression analysis was utilized to further narrow down the selection to the top five most representative genes connected with butyrate, namely CDKN3, CPS1, ABCC2, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1 (Fig. 2). We anticipate that these genes will serve as crucial indicators of patient survival.

Physicians have the ability to develop individualized treatment plans by utilizing the patient’s risk score, which allows for a more precise and convenient prediction of patient survival. We computed a risk score for each patient by evaluating the expression levels of these five crucial genes. We then divided the patients into high-risk and low-risk groups based on the median risk score. Finally, we developed a risk model. Our findings indicate that patients in the high-risk category had a poorer prognosis, indicating that the predictive risk model can partially predict patient survival. In order to further confirm the accuracy of the model’s predictions, we performed univariate regression analysis, multivariate regression analysis, and ROC curve analysis (Fig. 2). The results demonstrated that the risk signature, which is based on BMR-DEGs, can independently predict the prognosis of LUAD, indicating the trustworthiness of the model. For the purpose of determining whether or not the model has the capacity to generalize, the GSE68465 dataset was utilized as the test set for the purpose of external validation. The findings were in line with those of the TCGA-LUAD cohort, providing further evidence of the model’s predictive efficacy. Furthermore, we developed a nomogram using patient characteristics and clinicopathological factors. We then generated ROC curves at 1, 2, and 3 years to assess the accuracy of the model in predicting overall survival in patients with LUAD (Fig. 3). The results presented a numerical evaluation of the model’s ability to anticipate outcomes and further showcased its usefulness.

This study showcased the influence of genes involved in butyrate metabolism on the immunological microenvironment of LUAD. The findings indicated notable disparities in TIDE [30], Exclusion [31], and Dysfunction scores [32] between the two groups (Fig. 4), suggesting variations in the immunological microenvironment of LUAD between the two groups. These findings enhance our comprehension of the intricate immunological milieu in LUAD. Additionally, the utilization of this method can enhance the accuracy of predicting patients’ prognosis and risk, thereby establishing a foundation for personalized treatment. In addition, the results of this investigation revealed that there were significant differences in the number of immune cells that were present between the two groups of samples (Fig. 4). These disparities likely indicate the distribution and function of distinct immune cell types inside the lung adenocarcinoma microenvironment. This unique risk prediction algorithm can assist in forecasting patient treatment results. It was shown that the low-risk group had a greater abundance of a number of immune cells, including quiescent dendritic cells, CD4 memory quiescent T cells, and quiescent mast cells. These immune cells were all associated with higher survival rates.The high-risk group had a considerable enrichment of M0 macrophages and CD4 memory-activated T cells, which are associated with a poorer prognosis. The variation in prognosis among LUAD patients may be attributed to the diversity of the tumor microenvironment (TME), which offers novel avenues for our next investigations. Elevated levels of resting dendritic cells (RDCs) can secrete substances that entice tumor cells to gather at tumor locations. Dendritic cells play a crucial role in delivering antigens and activating adaptive immune responses [33]. Tumor cells can trigger the memory response of CD4 memory resting T lymphocytes by releasing certain chemicals. This prompts them to rapidly mobilize and migrate to the tumor site in order to assist the adaptive immune response in combating tumor growth. Upon reexposure to the same antigen, these memory T cells are capable of initiating a stronger and more effective immune response [34]. The elevated presence of quiescent mast cells within tumors may be attributed to the unique characteristics of the tumor microenvironment. Mast cells are a crucial type of immune cell. They have the capability to secrete a diverse range of bioactive compounds, including histamine, prostaglandins, and other cytokines, in order to modulate inflammation and the immunological response. These chemicals have the potential to stimulate mast cells in the tumor microenvironment, which can lead to the promotion of tumor development and metastasis [35]. The presence of M0 macrophages in the tumor microenvironment can enhance tumor progression and lead to a negative prognosis. This is because tumor cells have the ability to influence these macrophages, causing them to transform into M2 macrophages, which in turn promotes tumor growth and the spread of cancer cells [36].

Recent years have witnessed substantial advancements in tumor immunotherapy. Immune checkpoint inhibitors represent a significant milestone in the field of tumor immunotherapy. However, their effectiveness in treating LUAD remains highly restricted [37]. The increased expression of immune checkpoints PD-L1, PD-L2, and PD-1 in individuals with lung cancer may be associated with the immune evasion mechanism. Tumor cells may enhance the expression of these checkpoints, allowing them to evade detection and attack by the immune system. This, in turn, facilitates the growth and advancement of the tumor [38]. The expression levels of immunological checkpoints PD-L1, PD-L2, and PD-1 were significantly higher in the high-risk group and showed a positive correlation with the risk score (Fig. 5). This discovery suggests that groups at a higher risk may exhibit a more favorable reaction to immunotherapy.

In order to investigate the regulation mechanisms of important genes such as CPS1, ABCC2, CDKN3, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1, we created the ceRNA network. Ultimately, we established a ceRNA network consisting of 49 nodes and 77 edges, which establishes a connection between CDKN3 and hsa-mir-146b (Fig. 6). hsa-mir-5581 influenced the expression of IGFBP1. hsa-mir-32 controls the expression of CPS1. Prior research has discovered that miR-146a-5p decreases the expression of CDKN3 and specifically interacts with it, contributing to the progression of primary clear cell renal cell carcinoma without metastasis to tumors that generate distant metastases [39]. Inhibition of long non-coding RNA PVT1 inhibits the proliferation of Raji cells via regulating the function of cell cycle-related genes, such as CDKN3 [40]. Furthermore, certain research has indicated that lncRNA NEAT1 may have a safeguarding function in human umbilical vein endothelial cells via controlling the miR-181d-5p/CDKN3A axis [41]. The aforementioned studies demonstrate that constructing and predicting a ceRNA network can stimulate fundamental research on cancer and offer theoretical backing for novel targets and ideas in cancer diagnosis and treatment. This facilitates more focused subsequent basic verification and clinical research, avoiding aimless experimental exploration and minimizing the squandering of scientific research resources.

Within this set of genes, certain ones have been demonstrated to be connected to the occurrence and progression of cancerous tumors. It has been verified that changes in the expression of the CPS1 gene are linked to resistance to paclitaxel, a chemotherapy drug. Additionally, an elevated level of CPS1 expression may serve as a predictive biomarker for the unfavorable survival outcomes of individuals with epithelial ovarian cancer [42]. ABCC2, a protein associated with multidrug resistance, is highly expressed in various types of human malignancies and is increased in A549/DDP cells, which are resistant to cisplatin (DDP). A study has demonstrated that inhibiting ABCC2 can enhance the sensitivity of A549/DDP cells to DDP, halt their growth in the G1 phase, activate PARP and caspase-3, and improve the efficacy of DDP in eliminating subcutaneous A549 tumors in living organisms [43]. Increased expression of SLC2A1 is associated with a poorer prognosis, enhanced development of cancer cells, reduced presence of immune cells (including CD8 T cells and B cells), and a low prognostic nutritional index, which indicates the body’s nutritional state [44]. Tumor cells increase the expression of Insulin-like Growth Factor Binding Protein 1 (IGFBP1) specifically under limited movement within a confined space. IGFBP1 secretes a substance that prevents AKT1 from phosphorylating serine 27 of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2) and increases the activity of SOD2 [45].

Furthermore, CDKN3 is crucial in the control of carcinogenesis and development. The gene is located at position 14q22 and codes for the CDKN3 protein. Prior research has indicated that the expression of CDKN3 is increased in cervical cancer and is linked to a reduced survival time. This suggests that CDKN3 could serve as a possible biomarker for patients with cervical cancer [46]. CDKN3 exhibits high levels of expression in bladder cancer tissues and enhances both cell proliferation and migration. LDHA has a crucial role in modulating bladder cancer treatment resistance by mediating CDKN3, as stated in reference [47]. A study conducted on individuals diagnosed with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) revealed a noteworthy elevation in the CDKN3 mRNA level among ESCC patients. This rise was determined to have a strong correlation with lymph node metastases and the clinical stage of patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Additionally, it displayed a negative correlation with disease-free survival and overall survival rates [48]. Suppression of CDKN3 did not have a substantial impact on the growth of HCC cells, although it did decrease their responsiveness to doxorubicin [49]. Ovarian cancer often increases the expression of CDKN3. Furthermore, it is linked to signaling pathways that are connected to the cell cycle and the replication of DNA [50]. Deng et al. [51] showed that CDKN3 had a high level of expression in breast cancer cell lines, which resulted in the promotion of cell death and the inhibition of cell migration. Xu et al. [52] employed pathway analysis to investigate the genes that were expressed differently in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. The findings indicated that CDKN3 was increased in ESCC and played a crucial role as a pivotal gene in the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway and cell cycle.

The study findings indicate that CDKN3 is expressed at high levels in LUAD (Fig. 7). Furthermore, the study noted a substantial reduction in the growth, movement, and infiltration capabilities of A549 and H1299 cells following the suppression of CDKN3 (Figs. 8 and 9). These findings indicate that CDKN3 is likely to have a vital role in controlling the growth, movement, and infiltration of LUAD cells. Additional research is required to determine if the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway plays a role in regulating the proliferation, migration, and invasion of A549 cells and H1299 cells by CDKN3. Furthermore, our work is limited by the absence of block-recovery tests and animal experiments. In addition, although we collected a considerable number of samples, the sample size and diversity of this study may still limit the general applicability of the results, and the biomarkers identified in this study have not been fully validated in independent clinical cohorts. Therefore, we will continue to explore the role of these genes in the prognosis prediction of LUAD in future studies to further confirm their potential for clinical application.

In conclusion, this study is the first to elucidate the significant biological roles of a gene signature related to butyrate metabolism in predicting the prognosis of patients with LUAD. Notably, 5 BMR-DEGs (CPS1, ABCC2, CDKN3, SLC2A1, and IGFBP1) were identified as individual prognostic factors, and a nomogram was developed to predict the prognosis of LUAD patients. Furthermore, in vitro experiments indicated that inhibiting the expression of CDKN3 significantly suppressed the proliferation, migration, and invasion of LUAD cells. CDKN3 may serve as a novel prognostic indicator for LUAD.
